title: fetch and HTTP
summary: How fetch works, why a 404 is not an exception, JSON bodies and cancelling requests.

steps.title: fetch
body: `fetch` is the built-in HTTP client in browsers and Node, like `HttpClient`:
if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`);   // fetch does NOT throw on 404/500
const todo = await res.json();                         // parse the body: a second await
- `fetch` rejects only for **network** failures (offline, DNS, CORS blocked). Any HTTP status, even 500, fulfils. Check `res.ok` (status 200 to 299).
- The body can be read **once**: `res.json()`, `res.text()` or `res.blob()`.
- `res.json()` returns `any`. Treat it as `unknown` and validate it (module 5).
The exercises here cannot reach the network, so they pass in a fake `fetch` with the same shape.

steps.prompt: A request returns status 404. What does `await fetch(url)` do?
options: Fulfils with a Response whose `ok` is false and `status` is 404
steps.explain: Unlike `HttpClient.GetFromJsonAsync`, `fetch` treats any HTTP answer as a success. You must check `res.ok` yourself.

steps.title: Cancelling with AbortController
body: controller.abort();            // p rejects with an AbortError
React apps use this to cancel a request when the user leaves the page, and `AbortSignal.timeout(5000)` gives a signal that aborts on its own.
A typical loading flow has three states: **loading**, **error**, **data**. Module 8 shows how a component renders each one.

steps.prompt: Does `await fetch(url)` reject, or fulfil with a Response?
items: the DNS name does not exist

steps.prompt: Complete the code so it throws on HTTP errors and returns the parsed JSON.
This code throws `TypeError: Body is unusable` on the second line. Why?
options: A response body is a stream that can be read only once
`await` cannot be used twice in a row
steps.explain: Read the body once and keep the result: `const text = await res.text(); const data = JSON.parse(text);` lets you log the raw text and parse it.
